title: You Are Special
author: Doing Inclusion
summary: A special education teacher reflects on the twin human needs to belong and to be recognised as special. She draws on a communication book's premise that people want both, and shows how good teams and good inclusion hold the two together. Two student stories illustrate it: a student moved to a better-fit class who became calmer and could help others, and a student who toileted independently and held a first real two-way conversation once accepted in a class that expected routines and allowed processing time. She argues that what is special about special education is the staff who stay regulated, start from what a student can do and read early signs. For school leaders she asks whether staff feel they belong, suggests listing one personal and one special thing about every colleague, and urges quiet, genuine recognition.
points: People have two fundamental needs, to belong and to be recognised as unique, and the best teams and leaders balance both.
A move to a better-fit class transformed a student by letting them feel accepted and also valuable for what they could contribute.
Effective special educators stay calm, coregulate early and start from what the student can do instead of what they cannot.
School leaders are asked whether staff, not just students, feel they belong, especially the quiet people outside year-group teams.
Assumptions about behaviour are often wrong, and authentic recognition and quiet attention move people more than noise or false praise.
quotes: the basic premise that people have two fundamental needs - to belong and to be recognised for being special/unique.
Special education involves walking the tightrope of belonging and standing out with an incredible group of individuals who need you to see them, not their diagnoses.
It takes people who can start from the point that the student can, rather than the more common expectation in disability that they can’t.
When we start with can, we can then observe and plan for barriers and build in sensible scaffolds, not dumb things down, or lower expectations.
My question is whether your staff feel a sense of belonging, not just the students. Whether they feel appreciated for the special things they bring to the place they belong.
So often with behaviour, people jump to assumptions. I’ve learnt that often the assumption is wrong and you can identify this when you really know and work with the student.
Authentic, genuine, care, recognition and acknowledgement not false praise and noise to fill space are the drivers that will move people and make you memorable for your impact.
